Good morning. The Trump administration’s assault on the legitimacy of the midterm elections has continued, with the US president announcing a $1m reward for reports of voter fraud, amid several legal actions by the Department of Justice to limit voting.

Donald Trump said the bounty payment was contingent on the arrest and conviction of those responsible. He did not disclose how he would pay for the rewards. Trump’s comments follow his repeated and unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.

F-35 Fallacy: Jets Alone Will Not Save Us
item.description:
NATO Allies have bet the future of European skies on the world’s most sophisticated combat aircraft. NATO Allies are buying the world's most advanced fighter but many are neglecting vital investments in hard security, ground crews, and support systems that will keep it flying.

By 2028, European flight lines will host upwards of 700 F-35 Lightning jets. On paper, this inventory represents an insurmountable technological edge: a sensor-fused, fifth-generation fleet that outmatches any potential adversary in radar-cross-section, situational awareness, and electronic attack.

Yet this procurement spree masks a dangerous complacency. The Alliance has poured vast capital into acquiring fifth-generation airframes while systematically underinvesting in the unglamorous terrestrial infrastructure that keeps them flying: base hardening, counter-drone defenses, resilient networks, and ground crews. An F-35 sitting on an unhardened runway without fuel, parts, or secure command links is not a deterrent, it is an expensive target.

The cockpit may deliver tactical lethality, but operational endurance is generated entirely on the tarmac. If conflict erupts with Russia, the fight for European airspace will look less like a sterile, high-tech turkey shoot and more like the grueling attrition of the Battle of Britain.

Surviving Day Zero

Historically, the most efficient method of destroying an air force has rarely been in air-to-air combat; it has been catching it on the ramp. Operation Focus in 1967 wiped out Egypt’s air force before breakfast. Conversely, Ukraine averted immediate disaster in February 2022 because it aggressively dispersed its scarce aircraft and mobile air-defense batteries hours before Russian cruise missiles slammed into permanent garrisons.

Recent innovations have further collapsed the boundary between frontline and rear sanctuary. In June 2025, Ukraine demonstrated the democratization of deep strike with Operation Spiderweb, deploying commercial-style drones smuggled deep into the Russian interior to strike strategic bombers parked in the open. The threat bypassed layered air defense belts entirely; it originated outside the airbase perimeter fence. Coupled with intelligence reports of sabotage devices targeting logistical hubs in Western Europe, such as the attempted strikes near Leipzig, the implication for NATO is clear: rear sanctuary no longer exists.

Russia has studied these dynamics carefully. A coordinated "Day Zero" assault will not rely solely on long-range Iskander or Kalibr barrages. It will combine standoff salvos with covert proxy drone launches, special reconnaissance sabotage, and electromagnetic disruption targeting key airbases before any formal declaration of Article 5. If NATO’s F-35 fleet remains concentrated at sprawling, unhardened hubs, the Alliance risks losing the air war before its pilots can take off.

Survival on Day Zero will not come from a single system. Ground-based air defense will kill aircraft, cruise missiles will crater runways, and drones will hunt anything left in the open. The answer is dispersal, concealment, and resilience, practiced and exercised daily long before the shooting starts.

A Battle of Britain, Not a High-Tech War in the Air

The operational template NATO must internalize is not Desert Storm, but southern England in the summer of 1940. When the Luftwaffe hammered RAF sector stations across Kent and Sussex - cratering Biggin Hill, Manston, and Kenley - the British survived because of an integrated, highly resilient system.

It was not the Spitfire alone that preserved Britain; it was the Dowding System. Radar stations, visual observers, filter rooms, and telephone lines fused intelligence into an actionable operational picture and directed scarce interceptors to precise intercept vectors. Crucially, the system was distributed and made redundant. When individual nodes went dark, the architecture adapted. Meanwhile, exhausted ground crews patched runways and re-armed aircraft under constant threat of bombardment.

NATO faces an analogous network challenge today. The F-35 is a formidable intelligence-collection platform, but its utility plummets if its Multifunction Advanced Data Link (MADL) cannot pass target tracks to legacy fourth-generation fighters, naval surface combatants, or ground-based air defenses under heavy electronic jamming. If a Combined Air Operations Center (CAOC) is knocked offline, who assumes control of the theater airspace? Without distributed, jam-resistant data architectures and mission command protocols for degraded environments, tactical technological dominance will dissolve into operational paralysis.

Operational Imperatives for NATO Airpower

If NATO intends to build genuine deterrence by denial, member states must balance platform acquisition with systemic survivability across five core areas:

  1. Institutionalize Dispersal and Agile Combat Employment (ACE): Finland and Sweden have long mastered highway-strip operations, rapid turnaround, and camouflage doctrine. These must cease to be High North novelties and become standard operating procedure across all Allied air forces. Peacetime operations must routinely exercise dispersed sortie generation from municipal airports and road networks.
  2. Harden the Perimeter and the Flight Line: Every euro invested in advanced airframes must be matched by funding for base survivability: point-defense against low-altitude UAS, hardened aircraft shelters, mobile arrestor gear, rapid airfield damage repair (RADR) kits, and deep magazines of precision munitions.
  3. Expand Logistics at Strategic Depth: Dispersed operating locations demand rapid logistics and robust aerial refueling capacity. Staging fighters farther from the contact line requires a dramatic expansion of NATO’s multinational tanker fleet and hardened pipeline distribution networks.
  4. Solve the Cross-Domain Data Mesh: Allies must field resilient, low-probability-of-intercept gateways that translate fifth-generation sensor data into common operational pictures accessible to non-stealth assets and ground-based integrated air and missile defense systems. They also need the ability to protect and secure their entire EW spectrum, given the F-35's massive reliance on it.
  5. Re-arm and Re-train the Ground Crew: The maintainer, armorer, and combat engineer are frontline combatants. NATO must equip ground personnel with specialized force-protection capabilities, chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear defense gear, and the cross-training required to generate combat sorties in austere, contested conditions.

The True Cost of Deterrence

Deterrence is not measured by the sophistication of one platform; it is measured by the credible ability to absorb a first strike and generate combat power under fire. Building that credibility requires realistic, high-tempo exercises in harsh weather, degraded communications environments, and austere road bases. It must be under conditions that carry legitimate operational risk and wear on equipment.

Before 1989, this operational friction was the routine cost of doing business in Allied Air Forces Central Europe. The pilots of 1940 earned their place in history, but unheralded mechanics, plotters, and engineers preserved their freedom to fight. As NATO retools for contested collective defense, it must remember that fifth-generation air power is only as resilient as the ground beneath its wheels.

item.title: Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy
item.description:
Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy Expert comment jon.wallace 28 October 2026

The KDP and PUK largely agree on Kurdish issues in Turkey, Iran and Syria. But division on how to govern at home could invite outside interference and undermine hard-won self-governance.

Two years after Iraq’s Kurdistan Region went to the polls to elect a new government, the KDP and the PUK – the region’s two largest parties – have still failed to reach an agreement to form the new government. A caretaker government, originally elected in September 2018, remains in charge.

This situation is taking the Kurdistan Region down a path of profound and possibly permanent division. Its longstanding partners in Europe and the US have grown frustrated with its latent dysfunction and are no longer willing to play referee. This leaves it more vulnerable to interference from regional powers who are better placed to adapt and can play a longer game.

The main impediment to moving forward is not petty disagreements between the two parties over ministerial positions, as is sometimes claimed. Instead, the impasse stems from the collapse of the 2006 Strategic Agreement between the KDP and the PUK. The parties no longer share the same basic vision for how the Kurdistan Region should operate. The formal and informal frameworks that bound the two parties together for the last two decades are no longer functioning.

Instead, the Kurdistan Region has effectively divided into two geographic areas that are controlled by one party or the other. The KDP is in charge in Erbil and Duhok governorates. The PUK is dominant in Sulaymaniyah and Halabja.

The two zones are not fully separate, as they were during the era of divided administrations between 1998 and 2005. But it is a cumbersome arrangement. State institutions and the security forces look to unelected party leaders for guidance, not Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) ministries. Reports indicate that rents are extracted from truckers and traders at checkpoints on the border between KDP and PUK areas.

Until now, the parties have maintained that the Kurdistan Region remains a cohesive entity despite the partisan divide. On 6 October, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called on the parties to reactivate Kurdistan’s Parliament, which has not had a substantive meeting in more than four years saying: ‘I don’t know what they are afraid of’.

Below the surface, however, bigger changes may be afoot.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

Political leaders from the PUK have a more radical proposal: to devolve administrative and fiscal authority to governorates, mayors, and district directors. Some powers would be retained by the KRG and the Kurdistan Parliament. But most important decisions over everyday matters would be shifted to lower levels of governance. Proponents of the plan cite Switzerland’s cantons and the UAE’s emirates as inspiration. Better to get out of each other’s way, the argument goes, and disaggregate executive authority.

Given the outsized power wielded – exclusively and separately – by the two parties at the governorate and local levels, this change would formalize partisan control over governance within the Kurdistan Region’s two zones, representing the biggest constitutional change in a generation. 

And it would repudiate the key peacebuilding assumption following the Kurdish civil war: that strong, unitary, and shared institutions are needed to reinforce Kurdish self-government and autonomy. That it is even being considered reflects the depths to which relations between the KDP and the PUK have deteriorated.

Many parts of the plan are vague. How would it change the relationship between local authorities, the federal government, and the KRG? How will revenues be shared, if at all? How will decisions be made about key sectors like oil, gas, electricity, and trade?

For the moment this remains a PUK proposal, its prospects uncertain. The KDP opposes the plan – part of the reason there has been little progress in negotiations to form a government. Many Kurdish voters will oppose reinforcing the power of the ruling parties without any meaningful checks. And, while they are certainly disillusioned by their present circumstances, they are keenly aware of the risks the PUK plan would pose to the Kurdistan Region’s fragile constitutional position in Iraq.

Over the past five years, Iraq’s federal government has gradually eroded the KRG’s ability to manage its own political and economic affairs, enabled by the KDP and the PUK disunity. 

A bad time for division

The potential for a fracture inside the Kurdistan Region comes at an inopportune time geopolitically. The US–Iran War has created significant instability. Foreign partners are preoccupied with problems at home. And changing regional dynamics are seeing sovereign states reassert influence over non-state actors.

The US presence in the Kurdistan Region is less potent than in years past. It completed a military withdrawal at the end of September after twelve years as part of the international coalition fighting Islamic State. Diplomatic activity in Erbil – where the KRG is based – has been hampered for much of this year due to security concerns stemming from the US–Iran war.

American and European diplomats are discouraged by their inability to bring the KDP and the PUK together, despite restlessly encouraging them to form a government. This inability is a signal of the West’s flagging influence over top Kurdish leaders. That will only worsen if diplomats have to contend with empowered local officials that answer primarily to the KDP and the PUK leadership.

The Kurdistan Region’s immediate neighbours like Turkey and Iran are much better placed to adapt to a Kurdistan Region that is divided and disaggregated. They can play the long game, and act at the local level through economic, social, and religious ties, rather than the top-down military and political approach of the US and Europe. Unity between the KDP and the PUK matters far less in their calculations.

Turkey’s immediate aim in the Kurdistan Region is to ensure that its own Kurdish political process, which is seeing the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) disarm, continues. The KDP and the PUK have strongly supported this process and provided important interventions to facilitate it. They have also supported the integration process of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the new Syrian state. 

In the near-term, the KDP and the PUK are unlikely to diverge much from this path. But the risk is that greater division at home could fragment their positions on issues beyond the Kurdistan Region’s borders. If that happens, Ankara might side with one of the parties, which would result in further instability.

Iran’s first goal is to ensure that Kurdish groups do not enter its war with the US. So far, the KDP and the PUK are in lockstep about the importance of avoiding any impression that they might intervene against Iran. Tehran’s second goal is to curtail the activities of its own Kurdish armed groups, even to the point of demanding they be expelled from Iraq’s Kurdistan Region. Weak and divided state institutions in the KRG make this difficult to achieve. That, in turn, makes it more likely that Iran will take matters into its own hands.

In the absence of a US security presence, interference from regional neighbours could also lead Iraqi leaders in Baghdad to become more hands-on in dealing with matters in the Kurdistan Region. This would be a bad outcome for Kurdish self-governance and would likely inflame political tensions between the KDP and the PUK.

The sour mood that prevailed in the Kurdistan Region during the election two years ago has only deepened. Pushing governance decisions to the local level in an effort to avoid intractable partisan impasse at the top is one proposal. But it could have significant knock-on effects.  

A continued impasse between the KDP and the PUK risks setting off an irreversible decline for the frameworks that have enabled Kurdish self-governance for the past two decades. To get beyond this blockage, leaders from the KDP and the PUK must entertain imaginative solutions, but not ones that further divide, weaken its shared institutions or undermine democratic principles. Otherwise, it risks becoming a place that other actors pick apart at the expense of Kurdish autonomy.

item.title: Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
Once the midterms are over, Trump will be free to pursue vendetta politics. But with will and diplomacy, he can be reined in

As another Iran catastrophe looms, one question matters more than any other: how to stop it before it’s too late? Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming the illegal war of choice they began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.

Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut a treacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putin but, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. Trump also reportedly rebuffed last-gasp, electorally driven pressure from Netanyahu to hit Iran this month, fearful it would unleash a Democratic tsunami.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today sought Japan’s cooperation in diversifying Bangladesh’s export products, expressing hope that stronger economic ties would open up new avenues for trade and investment between the two countries.

He sought Japan’s cooperation during a meeting with Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) President Susumu Kataoka here at 11:45 am local time, said Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin.

During the meeting, the discussions focused on increasing Japanese investment in Bangladesh, diversifying exports, developing skills and strengthening bilateral trade and economic partnership.

Tarique Rahman appreciated JETRO’s role in promoting Japanese investment in Bangladesh, saying, “New opportunities for Japanese investment are emerging in Bangladesh.”

He said Bangladesh expected Japanese investment in manufacturing industries, information and communication technology (ICT), automobiles, renewable energy and agro-processing in the country’s special economic zones.

Both sides agreed that the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) would play an important role in strengthening trade and investment ties between the two countries.

The Prime Minister also urged Japan to cooperate in skills development programmes and the establishment of Japanese language training centres in Bangladesh. Such initiatives would help create employment opportunities in Japan and further strengthen the long-term economic partnership between the two countries, said the premier.

JETRO President Susumu Kataoka described Bangladesh as a promising investment destination, citing its economic growth and geographical location.

He said various initiatives taken by the government under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had already generated interest among Japanese companies in doing business and investing in Bangladesh.

Following the meeting, the Prime Minister attended a luncheon hosted by Kataoka. They also discussed ways to advance mutual cooperation and economic relations.

Tarique Rahman invited the JETRO president to visit Bangladesh at a time convenient to him.

item.title: Metro rail: Formal work kicks off for stations, tracks construction of 2 new routes
item.description:
Eight elevated stations and 11 kilometers of elevated tracks will be constructed for two new metro rail lines under four packages.

Contractors have been appointed for the construction of stations and railway tracks for MRT Line-1 (from the capital's Airport to Kamalapur) and MRT Line-5 (Northern Route, from Hemayetpur to Bhatara).

Additionally, various depot infrastructures will also be developed in Hemayetpur and Purbachal. The appointment of contractors marks the formal commencement of the construction of these stations and railway tracks.

Contracts under the four separate packages were signed on Tuesday (27 October) afternoon at the Metro Rail Bhaban in Diabari, Uttara. The two projects are being implemented by Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited (DMTCL) with joint financing from the Bangladesh government and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).

The total cost for constructing these two metro rail lines will be Tk 2 trillion. Of this, Tk 1.14 trillion will be spent on MRT Line-1 and Tk 890 billion on MRT Line-5.

MRT Line-1 will be 31 kilometers long, while MRT Line-5 will span 20 kilometers.

The metro rail line from Airport to Kamalapur will have 21 stations. The line from Hemayetpur to Bhatara will have 14 stations. Construction of both lines is scheduled to be completed by 2033.

Mohammad Ziaul Haque, secretary of the Road Transport and Highways Division attended the contract signing ceremony as the chief guest. Planning Commission Member (Acting Secretary) Kabir Ahmed was present as the special guest.

DMTCL Managing Director Md. Shaugatul Alam, along with representatives from the Embassy of Japan, JICA, project officials, consultants and contracting firms, were also present on the occasion, DMTCL said in a press release.

Works under 4 packages

According to the DMTCL press release, a total of 49 structures will be constructed for the MRT Line-1 depot under the agreement. This will include workshops, stabling sheds and an operation management centre.

The contract for this work was signed with China's Sinohydro and SEBCL. In addition, the contract for constructing a five-kilometre elevated viaduct and three stations (Joar Sahara, Boalia and Mastul) on this line was signed with China's CREC and MBEC and Japan's MIL.

For the MRT Line-5 depot, an agreement was signed with Taiwan's CPC and South Korea's Hanil to construct various infrastructures, including an administrative building, stabling yard, warehouse and workshop sheds.

Under another package, a contract was signed with CREC-MIL-MBEC for constructing a total of 6.50 kilometers of elevated railway from Hemayetpur to Aminbazar and from Natun Bazar to Bhatara, alongside five stations: Hemayetpur, Baliyapur, Bilamalia, Aminbazar and Bhatara.

The press release stated that implementing these four packages will advance the expansion of the capital's metro rail infrastructure.

Speaking at the ceremony, Road Transport and Highways Division Secretary Mohammad Ziaul Haque said that easing traffic congestion and reducing commute times in Dhaka remain one of the government's top priorities. To this end, the metro rail network is being expanded to build a modern, safe, and environmentally friendly mass transit system.

item.title: PM invites Japanese firms to explore five sectors for investment in Bangladesh
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today invited Japanese companies to explore investment opportunities in five priority sectors in Bangladesh-automotive manufacturing, energy, technology and space cooperation, rail and logistics, and agro-processing and manufacturing-to translate long standing bilateral ties into stronger trade and investment.

"I invite Japanese companies to explore five key areas for future cooperation and business opportunities for mutual benefits," he said while delivering the keynote speech at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum Dialogue at JETRO Hall in Tokyo.

Highlighting the untapped potential of bilateral economic ties, the Prime Minister said around 350 Japanese companies operate in Bangladesh, while Japanese direct investment in the country remains below US$500 million.

"Our exports to Japan reached 1.36 billion US dollars and Bangladesh imported from Japan 2.16 billion US dollars, in the last fiscal year," he said, stressing the need to take the relationship beyond development cooperation and expand trade and investment.

Recalling the longstanding friendship between the two countries, Rahman said Japan was among the first countries to recognise Bangladesh in February 1972 and had remained its largest development partner for more than five decades.

He also recalled the contributions of his parents-- Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and late Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia-- who visited Japan several times and helped deepen bilateral relations.

"Today, I want to speak about the next 30-50 years of partnership and collaboration," he said.

Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh and Japan had signed an Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) this year, the first such agreement Bangladesh had concluded with any country. Under the agreement, 7,379 Bangladeshi products will enjoy duty-free access to Japan, while Japanese goods, including steel, automotive parts and electronic components, will receive preferential access to Bangladesh.

The Prime Minister highlighted Bangladesh''s market of more than 180 million people, its young and energetic workforce with a median age of 27, and its growing middle class as major advantages for investors.

He said Bangladesh was expected to become one of the world''s top 10 consumer economies by 2030.

Identifying automotive manufacturing as the first priority, Tarique Rahman welcomed Toyota's plan, conveyed earlier this month, to begin work on a vehicle manufacturing facility in Bangladesh, with full production targeted by 2029. He assured the company of the government's full support.

In the energy sector, he invited Japanese companies to invest in liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure, efficient gas-fired power generation and renewable energy.

He said Bangladesh had short-, medium- and long-term plans for gas, electricity and the wider energy sector, and urged Japanese firms to explore the opportunities, noting that Bangladesh was working closely with JERA.

On technology and space cooperation, the premier said Bangladesh was planning to establish a Bangladesh-Japan Technology Park, including an innovation-focused information technology park covering artificial intelligence, cloud computing, robotics and electronics manufacturing, with the involvement of Japanese companies, universities and investors.

He said the two countries also had significant potential for cooperation in space technology. Bangladesh wanted to strengthen its space capabilities and was keen to explore mutually beneficial collaboration with Japanese institutions, drawing on Japan's experience in space science, technology and satellite engineering.

The Prime Minister identified rail and logistics as another priority, saying Bangladesh planned to build a nationwide elevated high-speed rail network connecting major cities, including Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet, Rajshahi, Khulna and Barishal.

"We plan to build a national network master plan, develop passenger and freight demand analysis, route prioritisation and feasibility studies. We will very much welcome Japanese institutions to invest in this critical and priority initiative," he said.

In agro-processing and manufacturing, the Prime Minister invited Japanese companies to explore food-processing opportunities in Bangladesh, which produces a wide variety of crops, fruits and vegetables.

"Japanese companies can explore opportunities in food processing in Bangladesh. We invite Japanese companies to invest in the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone at Araihazar. Sumitomo Corporation is developing this zone to Japanese standards," he said.

The Prime Minister said Bangladesh was working to address concerns raised by Japanese companies about reliable energy, efficient infrastructure, and predictable customs clearance and taxation.
"We have listened. We are working to address these concerns and deliver better outcomes," he said, adding, "I fully understand that businesses need certainty. Investors need confidence. Our job is creating the right environment to deliver both."

Emphasising people-to-people ties and skills development, Tarique Rahman said Bangladeshi students travelled to Japan every year for higher education, gaining valuable skills and experience before returning home.
He said teaching Japanese to Bangladeshi students was a government priority and outlined a vision of millions of young people learning the Japanese language alongside technical skills.

The premier said highly skilled Bangladeshi professionals with Japanese-language proficiency could help meet employment needs in both Japan and Bangladesh.

"Japan stood beside Bangladesh as we built our foundations. Now, we invite you to build our industries, create new opportunities, and grow together," he said.

The premier added, "Let us turn our longstanding friendship into a stronger partnership. Let us create mutual opportunities for our people, and prosperity for both of our nations."

The Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum Dialogue was organised by the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) in cooperation with the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Co-operation (JBCCEC), with support from the Bangladesh Embassy in Japan.

JETRO President Susumu Kataoka delivered the opening remarks, while Japan''s Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Shinji Wakayama addressed the event as a guest speaker. The programme also featured an MoU exchange ceremony and announcements of investment and cooperation projects.

Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury spoke on building an investment-led economy in Bangladesh, while Invest Bangladesh Chairman Ashik Chowdhury presented reforms and new initiatives to facilitate investment in Bangladesh.

Kenichiro Kawamoto, branch general manager and country chairperson of Mitsui & Co. (Asia Pacific) Pte. Ltd.''s Dhaka branch, delivered a presentation titled "Together for a Brighter Bangladesh". Reisuke Aratani, vice-president of YKK Corporation''s Global Sales Headquarters, presented the company''s business journey in Bangladesh and its future prospects.
Prime Minister''s Adviser Rehan Asif Asad also spoke on high-growth emerging businesses in Bangladesh.

Home minister: No need to amend constitution to prevent enforced disappearances
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said there is no need to introduce new provisions in the constitution to prevent enforced disappearances, noting that Article 32 already guarantees the right to life and that legislation has been enacted to prevent and address such cases.
“Article 32 of the Constitution recognises the right to life. Laws have already been enacted to prevent and address enforced disappearances. However, the necessary legal measures must be ensured to prevent anyone from becoming a victim of enforced disappearance in the future,” he said.
He made the remarks at a press briefing at the parliament’s media centre on Wednesday, following a meeting of the Special Committee on Constitutional Amendments in the cabinet room of the National Parliament. Salahuddin chairs the committee.
The minister said relatives of victims and representatives of people who had returned after being forcibly disappeared were invited to share their experiences and concerns with the committee.
He said the families and representatives had a common demand: ensuring that no one is subjected to enforced disappearance in the future.
According to Salahuddin, the committee invited family members of people who were subjected to enforced disappearance, killing and torture during the Awami League government’s 17-year tenure, as well as representatives of those who had returned after disappearing. The Liberation War Affairs Ministry, Mayer Daak and several other organisations helped prepare a list of 48 representatives, he added.
The families included wives, children and parents of people who remain missing, the minister said. Committee members listened attentively as relatives called for speedy and fair trials, efforts to locate missing people, official recognition of their families and rehabilitation.
Some relatives were too emotional to finish speaking, he added.
Referring to Article 32, Salahuddin said those responsible for enforced disappearances had violated the constitution. He said further legislation could be enacted if necessary.
On compensation for victims and their families, the minister said the existing law on the prevention of and remedies for enforced disappearance provides for compensation.
Under the law, he said, compensation may be paid through the seizure and sale of the assets of those found responsible, subject to a court order. If the accused have no assets or compensation cannot be recovered from them, the state can provide compensation, he added.
Salahuddin said the law also provides for independent investigations. If a particular force or law enforcement agency is accused of enforced disappearance, the same force or agency will not investigate the allegation; another force will conduct the inquiry.
The law contains separate provisions for investigation and accountability, as well as disciplinary action and criminal proceedings, he said.
Asked about allegations of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings under the current government, Salahuddin said no such incidents had occurred during its eight months in office.
“Has there been any crossfire? Any extrajudicial killing? Any custodial death? Has anyone been subjected to enforced disappearance? Not a single one,” he said.
The committee chair said the government had investigated one allegation and had also invited international human rights organisations to conduct an independent inquiry.
Asked about the inspector general of police’s use of the term “crossfire”, Salahuddin said the wording might have been careless while referring to strict enforcement of the law. However, he said he had already made it clear that such terminology was inappropriate.
The minister said the committee would recommend incorporating into the constitution matters that require constitutional recognition, while issues that could be addressed through legislation or regulations would be dealt with accordingly.

item.title: How the Fed is likely to act on interest rates just days before the midterm elections
item.description:
The Federal Reserve is expected to stand pat on interest rates Wednesday even though inflation has accelerated in the past couple of months as the Iran war has caused spikes in oil and gas prices.

The Fed’s latest policy meeting concludes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items.

The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation. The Fed raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%, in what many investors and economists perceived was a first step toward a renewed effort to bring down inflation.

Yet Warsh faces a host of challenges in achieving that goal. President Donald Trump slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank’s rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed. And some of the forces driving inflation — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won’t easily be tamed by higher interest rates.

At the same time, other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans’ sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.

After the Fed announces its rate decision, Warsh will speak at a news conference, where his remarks will be closely watched for hints about the Fed’s next steps. He will likely repeat the Fed’s desire for a “timelier” return of inflation to the 2% target. Some may view that as a sign the Fed will boost its key rate at its next meeting, in December, a move already widely expected by Wall Street investors.

If the Fed keeps rates on hold, Warsh will be pushed to explain why the central bank hiked in September but not this month. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.

And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely-followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed’s 2% target.

On Thursday, a separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.

Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics at Bank of America, said economists and the Fed have gotten too complacent about above-target inflation. Higher oil and gas prices will likely keep inflation elevated for several more months, he said, and rising diesel costs will elevate shipping prices for nearly every type of good, which could spread inflation more broadly through the economy.

“Unless the Fed takes this problem more seriously and stops essentially making excuses about inflation, I think we’re not going to get back to 2% until the next recession,” Bhave said.

Warsh will likely seek to keep the Wednesday press conference relatively short. It was about 30 minutes last month. Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, often held news conferences for about 45 minutes.

The Fed’s policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.

For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.

Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren’t particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

—Christopher Rugaber, AP Economics Writer

item.title: Google and Apple hit with a combined fine of $47.6 million by South Korea’s watchdog
item.description:
South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet’s Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country’s media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems.

The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures.

Google and Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said.

The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023.

South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

—Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press

item.title: Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose
item.description:
Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose  Expert comment jon.wallace 29 October 2026

Either way, the UK will be forced to pay a price.

The EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is pushing the UK toward an economic confrontation with China it would rather avoid. The IAA plans to introduce new ‘Made in Europe’ obligations, conditioning access to certain public subsidy and procurement schemes on the use of sufficient local, European, content. This is intended, in part, to protect European industry from cheap, high-quality, Chinese goods such as hybrid and electric vehicles (EVs). 

The UK government, seeking closer economic integration with the EU, wants ‘Made in Europe’ provisions extended to include its firms. But key EU member states are conditioning any extension on the UK aligning with EU economic security measures. 

A 15 October Franco-German paper said that ‘Made in Europe’ treatment for the automotive sector should only be extended to the UK and a small group of other partners on the condition of both reciprocity and ‘dynamic alignment with EU conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defense measures’. 

In practical terms, France and Germany want the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs to prevent the further erosion of their manufacturers’ UK market share. They also want the UK to impose stricter conditions on foreign direct investment into key manufacturing sectors to prevent Chinese firms from qualifying for future EU subsidies or procurement schemes via their UK-located operations. 

With the next EU–UK summit scheduled for 20 November, this creates a problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new government. Much of the media reporting has focused on the question of whether the UK will agree to impose tariffs on Chinese vehicles. But the focus on investment is arguably more consequential, given the UK’s desire to attract Chinese automotive manufacturing facilities to Britain. 

The UK’s China problem

Until now, the UK’s preferred approach to China has been one of cautious pragmatism. It has demonstrated a willingness to intervene with tariffs or other restrictions in the event of acute economic or national security concerns. See, for example, the decision to impose permanently high tariffs on certain steel products or the blocking of a proposed £1.5 billion investment in offshore wind by the Chinese firm Ming Yang.

However, the UK has continued to court Chinese investment in the automotive sector and deepen trade ties in what it considers non-sensitive areas. And, though it has made a commitment to the US to strengthen supply chain security in respect of steel and pharmaceuticals as part of the 2025 Economic Prosperity Deal, there has so far been limited evidence of substantive implementation. 

The UK’s reluctance to fully align with either the EU or US approach to China is understandable, given its relative size and economic weight. It wants increased trade and investment and relies on Chinese renewables for its decarbonization objectives. 

But the UK can certainly not afford to be shut out of EU procurement and public subsidy schemes. The EU’s proposed safeguard on hybrid vehicle imports – which would restrict imports above specified quota levels – will also create its own pressures, as Chinese vehicles risk being diverted onto the UK market. 

It is therefore less of a question of whether the UK will align itself with EU economic security measures than how.

The price to pay

One route would be for the UK to replicate EU measures wholesale. This would see the UK replicate EU tariffs on EVs and the new hybrid safeguard. And it could potentially include future interventions targeting chemicals, plastics, batteries and wind turbines. 

The UK would also need to consider equivalent restrictions on foreign investment, reflecting proposed IAA conditions relating to ownership limits, joint ventures, workforce localization and local content in key manufacturing sectors. 

Yet this approach is not straightforward. The UK does not necessarily have the legal tools available to replicate EU measures and has historically been cautious about breaching its international obligations. 

China would also be incentivized to retaliate. That could mean anything from initiating its own tariff measures against UK exports to imposing restrictions on rare earths or battery inputs.

The UK is not the only country in the region facing pressure from the EU to impose more stringent controls on Chinese trade and investment as a condition for access to the EU market. Turkey, Morocco and Switzerland are in a similar position. China will be wary of a negative precedent being established and keen to demonstrate that aligning with EU restrictions comes at a price. Indeed, Beijing may have a greater incentive to make an example of the UK than escalate its confrontation with the EU.

An alternative would be for the UK to pursue similar outcomes more slowly, using traditional trade defence tools. An anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese electric vehicles, for example, would take around a year to conclude but could provide the government with some breathing space. A safeguard investigation, potentially justified by rising Chinese imports and the risk of trade diversion from the EU, could offer a quicker route. 

Neither would guarantee the outcome the EU wants. And both would need to satisfy the relevant legal requirements. But they would at least allow the UK to argue that it was responding to evidence of harm to its own industry, rather than simply implementing EU demands. 

A safeguard also has the benefit, or not, of generally applying to imports regardless of origin, allowing the UK to argue it is not singling out China. It also remains possible that Brussels will attach more importance to the political signal of alignment than to the precise form of the measures adopted.

Yet this still leaves open the question of Chinese investment into UK manufacturing. This is of particular importance in the automotive sector. And it will prove more difficult to address without compromising the government’s wider economic objectives.

The government could also seek to demonstrate progress by announcing new economic security tools, such as a proposed anti-coercion instrument. It could also introduce specific restrictions on foreign investment, or repackage existing initiatives, such as new cybersecurity-related restrictions. Such announcements might demonstrate goodwill towards Brussels but they would not automatically satisfy EU demands for alignment on specific measures. 

The most likely outcome is that the UK seeks to navigate a course through these competing demands, giving the EU just enough of what it wants, while delaying implementation, hoping to avoid the worst response from Beijing. Delay may buy time with Brussels. But Beijing will likely view any such commitment as setting a precedent and retaliate against the UK accordingly. 

There will be a price for the UK to pay either way. The only question is how successfully the government can minimize it.
